item.content:encoded:
US House Republicans choose Jim Jordan as their next party leader Reuters | Updated: 11-11-2026 01:36 IST | Created: 11-11-2026 01:36 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

House Republicans chose Jim Jordan on Tuesday to lead them in opposition to a Democratic-controlled Congress, according to a person familiar with the matter, putting a combative Donald Trump ally at the forefront of the party’s fight to defend the US president’s agenda during his final two years in office. A secret ballot held behind closed doors elevated the Ohio Republican and House Judiciary Committee chairman to the minority leadership post a week after Democrats swept to victory in last Tuesday's midterm elections, winning sizable majorities in both the House and Senate. House Speaker Mike Johnson opted not to stand for the leadership position. Across the Capitol, Senate Republicans met behind closed doors to decide whether to push forward with internal elections that were expected to retain US Senator John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, as the party leader or opt for a delay that could allow a challenger to emerge. The House and Senate leadership elections will help determine what role Republicans intend to play as the minority party in Congress during the final two years of Trump's presidency. Democrats will need Republican support to move major initiatives in the 100-member Senate, where the filibuster rule requires 60 votes for most legislation. Their majorities in both chambers also fall well short of the two-thirds votes needed to override presidential vetoes. After the midterm elections, Thune vowed that Republicans would work with Trump to block "Democrat extremism" and work against any attempt by Democrats to unwind Republican achievements including border security and judicial appointments. Jordan, 62, was first elected in 2006 to represent a deeply conservative rural district in northern Ohio and was a founder of the House Freedom Caucus, a group that former Republican Speaker John Boehner labeled "legislative terrorists." Before entering politics, Jordan honed his pugilistic style during a career as a high school and university champion wrestler, and later as a wrestling coach at Ohio State University. That past threatened his political career in 2018 when former students accused him of turning a blind eye to rampant sexual abuse of college wrestlers by the wrestling team's doctor, when Jordan was an assistant coach. Jordan denied all allegations, and a university investigation found no hard evidence that he knew of the abuse. But former wrestlers said the doctor's abuse was well-known and the report itself found that students had complained about the doctor's voyeurism in front of coaching staff. Jordan has often referred to his wrestling background in terms of his reputation as a fighter in Congress. He is known for his aggressive style of questioning in committee hearings. "I look at it like a wrestling match," Jordan told the New York Times in an April 2023 interview, explaining how he prepares for hearings. "I'm going to try to get as ready as I can. You can't just wing it."

item.content:encoded:
US Army member arrested in UK for suspected 'espionage' for Russia Reuters | Updated: 11-11-2026 01:30 IST | Created: 11-11-2026 01:30 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

A senior US Army soldier was arrested in Britain on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, British police said on Tuesday, after the US removed aircraft from British military bases over a separate apparent threat from Iran. FBI Director Kash Patel said the arrest of the 41-year-old man related to "allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies." Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, added: "The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent." The arrest, which took place near the city of Gloucester, west England, on Tuesday "is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations", British police said. But it occurred the day after the US removed refuelling aircraft from a British airbase in the second such apparent evacuation in three months. Planes left the Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall, eastern England on Monday which, according to the Wall Street Journal, was prompted by a threat from Iran. The US in September withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran from RAF Fairford on security grounds over an incident police have linked to Iran, which has denied any links to attacks or incidents in Britain. The US Army soldier arrested on Tuesday was detained on suspicion of offences under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Police said the country to which the allegations relate is Russia.

item.content:encoded:
US STOCKS-Wall St retreats as hot inflation data, Fed comments fuel rate worries Reuters | Updated: 11-11-2026 01:13 IST | Created: 11-11-2026 01:13 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US stocks stumbled on Tuesday, as a hotter-than-expected inflation reading cemented expectations for a rate hike from the Federal Reserve next month and fueled concerns the central bank may be more aggressive in raising rates. The Labor Department said the Consumer Price Index increased 0.4% last month, its third straight gain of 0.4% or more and above the 0.3% estimate of economists polled by Reuters, after advancing 0.6% in September. The data came after Fed Governor Christopher Waller said the central bank should raise short-term borrowing costs in December even if data shows inflation cooled last month, and should consider an upsized half-point rate hike if the inflation picture worsens. Markets are now completely pricing in a rate hike of at least 25 basis points at the Fed's December meeting, according to CME FedWatch, up from 84% on Monday. The two-year US Treasury yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Fed, surged 19.1 basis points to 4.738% and was on track for its biggest daily gain since April 9, 2025, after US President Donald Trump launched his sweeping global tariffs. The jump has come even as oil prices have eased to two-month lows as US officials have downplayed any imminent military actions against Iran. "What kind of has the market spooked a little bit is this idea of, 'Well, we were already pricing in a December hike ... but maybe it's not 25, maybe it's 50, and maybe the Fed's more worried about inflation than I am, so let's sell some stocks,'" said Jason Ware, chief investment officer at Albion Financial Group in Salt Lake City, Utah. "From our perch, that is irrational. The thing that has pushed CPI up over the last six months and has the Fed a little bit more concerned and therefore has restarted hiking rates is because we've seen oil, energy and diesel push through in terms of inflation. If we have oil now going the other way ... this is all going to settle down." The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 223.12 points, or 0.43%, to 52,166.63, the S&P 500 lost 48.06 points, or 0.64%, to 7,501.88 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 290.69 points, or 1.15%, to 24,962.44. TECHNOLOGY SECTOR UNDER PRESSURE The S&P 500 and Nasdaq had risen for two straight days, bouncing back from sharp losses last week sparked by concerns about the potential for government regulations slowing the AI buildout. The S&P 500 technology sector dropped more than 1% as the worst-performing of the 11 major sectors, weighed down by another drop in Nvidia, which fell more than 5% and has tumbled about 10% over the past two sessions. The company's stock reflects mounting concerns over CEO Jensen Huang's future at the chip company after it initiated an internal probe into spy claims involving Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The CEO's relationship with Alice Huang facilitated the shipment of at least $7.5 billion worth of the company's chips through Chinese firms, the Information reported on Tuesday. But declines for the broader Philadelphia semiconductor index were more muted, off roughly 1% after two consecutive sessions of gains, as volatility in the AI trade increased. Aside from Waller, other Fed officials speaking on Tuesday also took a hawkish tone. Dallas Federal Reserve President Lorie Logan said that the Fed needs to deliver at least two more quarter-percentage-point interest rate increases to bring down inflation, and may need to do so promptly, while Kansas City Federal Reserve President Jeff Schmid said he believes the current policy rate is "fairly accommodative." ANTHROPIC IPO LOOMS LARGE Investors are also bracing for Anthropic's expected public listing later this month. The AI lab revealed that its initial public offering is expected to raise as much as $64.4 billion, giving the company a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. A listing by Anthropic could also force other AI heavyweights to compete harder for investor dollars. Neocloud firm CoreWeave is expected to report quarterly earnings after the market close on Tuesday. Questions about the sustainability of the AI boom and the company's debt burden have pressured the stock recently, which was now down about 33% on the year. CoreWeave shares were off 2.3% on the session, while those of its peer Nebius tumbled more than 6%. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.53-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange, and by a 2.49-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted six new 52-week highs and three new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 50 new highs and 201 new lows.
